question_text: What are the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Indian Constitution and which one can be suspended during emergency?
correct_answer: Fundamental Rights are in Part III (Articles 12-35): Right to Equality (14-18), Right to Freedom (19-22), Right against Exploitation (23-24), Right to Freedom of Religion (25-28), Cultural and Educational Rights (29-30), Right to Constitutional Remedies (32). During national emergency under Article 352, rights under Article 19 are automatically suspended. Rights under Articles 20 and 21 (protection from arbitrary arrest and right to life) cannot be suspended even during emergency.
key_points: Six categories of Fundamental Rights in Articles 12-35
Article 19 automatically suspended during National Emergency
Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even in emergency
Article 32 is the 'heart and soul' — right to approach Supreme Court
tip: Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul of the constitution' — interviewers love this quote.

question_text: Explain the concept of basic structure doctrine. How did it emerge?
correct_answer: The basic structure doctrine holds that certain fundamental features of the Indian Constitution cannot be amended by Parliament even with a two-thirds majority. Emerged from Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973) — 13-judge bench ruled 7-6 that while Parliament can amend any provision, it cannot destroy the basic structure. Basic structure includes: supremacy of constitution, republican and democratic form, secularism, federalism, separation of powers, judicial review, and fundamental rights.
key_points: Kesavananda Bharati case 1973 — 13 judge bench, 7-6 verdict
Parliament cannot destroy basic structure even with 2/3 majority
Basic structure: supremacy, democracy, secularism, federalism, judicial review
Indira Gandhi government's attempt to override it in 42nd amendment overturned
tip: Mention Minerva Mills (1980) case where 42nd Amendment was struck down using basic structure doctrine.

question_text: What is the role and powers of the Governor in an Indian state?
correct_answer: Governor is the constitutional head of state appointed by the President (not elected). Executive powers: all executive action taken in Governor's name, appoints Chief Minister and Council of Ministers. Legislative powers: summons, prorogues, and dissolves State Legislature, gives assent to bills. Discretionary powers: appointing CM when no clear majority, reserving bills for President's consideration, recommending President's Rule under Article 356. The Governor acts on advice of Council of Ministers except in specific discretionary matters.
key_points: Appointed by President — agent of Centre
Ordinance-making power when legislature not in session
Article 356: recommend President's Rule in state
Discretionary: appointing CM when hung assembly
tip: Article 356 misuse is politically controversial — know the Sarkaria Commission recommendations on Governor's role.

question_text: What is the difference between a Money Bill and an ordinary bill in Parliament?
correct_answer: A Money Bill (Article 110) deals exclusively with taxation, borrowing by government, expenditure from Consolidated Fund, or appropriation of money. It can only originate in Lok Sabha, the Speaker certifies it, and Rajya Sabha can only return it with recommendations (not reject it) within 14 days — after which it is deemed passed. An ordinary bill can originate in either house, requires equal consent from both houses, and Rajya Sabha can delay it. Joint sitting resolves deadlock in ordinary bills but not Money Bills.
key_points: Money Bill: only in Lok Sabha, Speaker certifies, Rajya Sabha cannot reject
Rajya Sabha has 14 days — recommendations only, not amendments
Ordinary bill: both houses equal, joint sitting for deadlock
Finance Bill is broader than Money Bill — can go to Rajya Sabha
tip: Aadhaar Bill passed as Money Bill was controversially challenged — know this recent debate.

question_text: Explain the amendment procedure under Article 368 of the Indian Constitution.
correct_answer: Article 368 provides for three types of amendments. Simple majority (like ordinary legislation): admission of new states, creation of legislatures, citizenship. Special majority (2/3 of members present and voting + majority of total membership of each house): most constitutional amendments. Special majority + ratification by half of state legislatures: provisions affecting federal structure — election of President, executive power of Centre and states, Chapter IV of Part V, representation in Parliament, Supreme Court and High Courts. President must give assent — no veto.
key_points: Three procedures: simple, special majority, special + state ratification
Federal provisions need state legislature ratification by 50%
President must give assent — no option to withhold
24th Amendment made Article 368 explicit — Parliament can amend any part
tip: What triggered Article 368 debate: Golaknath case said FRs cannot be amended — overruled by Kesavananda Bharati.

question_text: What are Directive Principles of State Policy and how do they differ from Fundamental Rights?
correct_answer: DPSPs (Part IV, Articles 36-51) are guidelines to the state for framing laws and policies — they are non-justiciable (cannot be enforced in court). They include provisions for uniform civil code, free legal aid, living wage, equal pay, village panchayats, protection of environment, and international peace. Fundamental Rights are justiciable — courts can enforce them. Initially held that FRs override DPSPs when they conflict. After 42nd Amendment and Minerva Mills case, both must be harmoniously implemented.
key_points: DPSPs: non-justiciable, moral obligations on state
FRs: justiciable, enforceable in court
42nd Amendment: DPSPs cannot be challenged on grounds of violating FRs
Both must be harmoniously read — not absolutely superior to each other
tip: Part IV takes inspiration from Irish Constitution and Fabian socialism — show historical origin knowledge.

question_text: How is the President of India elected and what are the grounds for impeachment?
correct_answer: President is elected by an electoral college comprising elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of all state Legislative Assemblies (and UTs with legislatures). Value of each MLA vote depends on state population. Value of each MP vote is total MLA vote value divided by total elected MPs. Voting by single transferable vote with proportional representation. Impeachment: motion in either house, requires 14 days notice, two-thirds majority of total membership of both houses (different from ordinary special majority).
key_points: Electoral college: elected MPs + elected MLAs (not nominated)
MLA vote value: state population / (number of MLAs × 1000)
Impeachment: 2/3 of total membership of both houses
14 days notice required before impeachment motion
tip: Presidential election is indirect because framers feared direct election = populist president undermining parliamentary democracy.

question_text: What is the doctrine of separation of powers and how is it applied in India?
correct_answer: Separation of powers divides government into three independent branches: Legislature (law-making), Executive (enforcement), and Judiciary (interpretation). India does not follow strict separation — the Constitution has a parliamentary system where executive is drawn from and accountable to the legislature. However, functional separation exists: Parliament cannot perform judicial functions, courts cannot make laws, executive cannot override judicial decisions. India has checks and balances rather than strict separation.
key_points: India has checks and balances, not strict separation
Parliamentary system: executive from legislature — overlapping
Judiciary is independent — appointment and removal separate
No House of Commons like UK — Rajya Sabha provides second check
tip: Compare India's fusion of executive and legislative with USA's strict separation — good analytical point.

question_text: Explain the structure and jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India.
correct_answer: Supreme Court is the apex court comprising Chief Justice and up to 33 other judges. Original jurisdiction: disputes between states, between states and Centre, and fundamental rights (Article 32). Appellate jurisdiction: appeals from High Courts in civil, criminal, and constitutional matters. Advisory jurisdiction: President can seek opinion under Article 143. Supreme Court decisions are binding on all courts. Special Leave Petition (Article 136) allows appeal from any court or tribunal. Constitutional Bench: minimum 5 judges for constitutional interpretation.
key_points: CJI + 33 judges maximum (increased from 30 in 2019)
Original jurisdiction: centre-state disputes + Article 32 FR cases
Advisory jurisdiction under Article 143 for Presidential reference
Constitutional Bench: minimum 5 judges, binding on all courts
tip: Article 32 vs Article 226: Both for FR enforcement. Article 32 goes to SC, 226 to High Court.

question_text: What is the 73rd Constitutional Amendment and its significance for local governance?
correct_answer: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment (1992) gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj Institutions. Added Part IX and 11th Schedule. Key provisions: three-tier system (village, intermediate, district panchayat), five-year elections, reservation for SCs, STs, and women (1/3 seats), State Finance Commission to recommend fund devolution, State Election Commission for conducting elections, and 29 subjects listed in 11th Schedule for panchayats. Transformed local bodies from administrative units to democratic institutions.
key_points: 1992 amendment — gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj
Three tiers: Gram, Intermediate (Block), Zila Panchayat
Mandatory reservation: SC/ST proportional + 1/3 for women
11th Schedule: 29 subjects including agriculture, education, rural roads
tip: States can give more subjects than 29 but not less — state discretion in implementation causes uneven results.
